opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and one I think about a lot with the teams we work with at AI Fund.

My bias is that, especially in the early days, building a product users genuinely love is the thing to get right first. If you have something people really want, go-to-market gets much easier. Word of mouth starts working for you, and customers pull the product out of your hands. If the product isn't there yet, even a brilliant go-to-market motion mostly helps you find out faster that people don't want it, and it burns a lot of money along the way.

I wouldn't treat them as completely sequential, though. One thing I've seen work well is to be very concrete about who the customer is from day one. Don't say "we're building AI for healthcare." Say "we're building this for this kind of person, in this workflow, who has this specific pain." When you're that specific, product and go-to-market start to merge. You know who to talk to, where to find them, and what they'll pay for, and that feedback goes right back into the product.

With generative AI, the cost of building prototypes has dropped dramatically. Something that used to take a team months can now sometimes be built in days. So the bottleneck is shifting. It's less about whether we can build it and more about deciding what to build and getting it in front of users quickly. That raises the importance of product management and user feedback. If engineering is faster, you need to iterate on what users actually want much faster too.

So my rough rule of thumb is to obsess over the product and the user early on, with a clear picture of the customer. Once you see real pull, like people using it repeatedly, telling their friends, or asking to pay, that's when I'd lean much harder into scaling go-to-market. Doing it in the reverse order is one of the more common ways I've seen startups struggle.

r001.rationale: The response recommends getting a product users genuinely love right first, especially early on, before leaning into scaling go-to-market.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a mistake to treat those as two separate phases. Honestly, the thing I see teams get wrong most often is they spend months building something in isolation, and then they say, "okay, now let's figure out go-to-market." And by then they've already made a hundred decisions about the product that no customer ever weighed in on.

So the way I think about it, you really can't build something people love without being in the market early. At AI Fund, when we start a company, one of the first things we do is talk to a lot of potential customers, before there's much of a product at all. And then we try to get something in front of users very, very fast, in days or weeks, not months. The goal isn't to sell it yet. The goal is to learn. Because what people tell you in a conversation and what they do when they actually have the thing in their hands are often quite different.

Now, having said that, if I had to put weight on one side, I'd put it on building something users genuinely love. If you have a product that people really want, it's amazing how much a go-to-market can forgive. You can have a mediocre sales process and still grow, because customers pull it out of you. The reverse is much harder. I've seen very strong sales teams push a product that users were lukewarm about, and you get this illusion of traction for a while, and then churn catches up with you.

The other thing I'd say, especially now with AI, is that the cost of building a prototype has dropped dramatically. So the bottleneck has shifted. It used to be that engineering was the expensive part, so you'd be careful and plan a lot before you built. Now you can build quickly and cheaply, which means the scarce resource is really product judgment, knowing what to build. And the only way I know to develop that judgment is to be very close to users, constantly. So in that sense, early go-to-market, meaning just getting in front of real customers, is actually how you figure out what a lovable product even is.

r001.rationale: The response favors building a product users love if forced to choose, but it explicitly rejects doing that before go-to-market work: it recommends talking to customers and getting a prototype to users early to learn what to build.

astra-6.text:
I tend to start with creating something that users really want. But I think treating product and go-to-market as two separate things can be misleading. How you reach users, how they try the product, and how quickly they get value are all part of whether you can build a successful business.

With AI, one thing I encourage teams to do is get to a concrete prototype quickly. You can spend a lot of time debating an idea in the abstract, but putting something in front of a user often teaches you much more. Do they actually use it? Do they come back? Does it solve a problem they care enough about to pay for?

At the same time, I wouldn’t wait until the product is finished to figure out distribution. If you need a six-month enterprise sales process to sell something that generates a few hundred dollars a year, that’s a problem you want to discover early. So I would prioritize delivering user value, while testing the go-to-market assumptions alongside the product assumptions.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes delivering user value, but explicitly recommends testing go-to-market assumptions alongside product assumptions rather than building a product users love first and solving go-to-market afterward.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as tightly connected. You need to build something users love, but you also need a way to reach those users and learn from them. If you build in isolation and postpone go-to-market until the product is finished, you can spend a lot of time solving the wrong problem.

Early on, I would focus on a specific customer and a specific problem. Can you get a few people to use the product, get real value from it, and come back? Working directly with those customers is both product development and go-to-market. You learn what matters, how to explain the value, and who actually makes the purchasing decision.

Then, as you see evidence that the product is working, you can invest more in distribution. The balance depends on where the uncertainty is. If people try it and don't stick around, work on the product. If people love it but very few people discover it, work on reaching more of them.

r001.rationale: The response says product work and go-to-market should be tightly connected and happen together early, then recommends increasing distribution as the product shows evidence of working. It does not recommend building a product users love before solving go-to-market.
